  • Crude oil is no longer the protagonist: the next energy crisis is quietly brewing in refineries.

Crude oil is no longer the protagonist: the next energy crisis is quietly brewing in refineries.

wallstreetcn ·  May 11 14:00
BZcurrent +1.19%
BZmain +1.19%

JPMorgan analyst Kaneva pointed out that the pressure from the current round of the energy crisis has shifted from crude oil to refined product segments. The increase in refined product prices in Asia has reached 1.5 to 3 times that of crude oil, with aviation fuel crack spreads surging to $80 to $100 per barrel. Global crude oil inventories are expected to fall to the 'operational bottom line' by September, while limited refining capacity is exacerbating supply gaps. The next phase of impact will manifest in the form of refined product shortages, directly affecting aviation, logistics, and consumers.

While the market is still questioning why oil prices have failed to break out into a rally, the real energy shock has quietly shifted its focus.

Natasha Kaneva, a commodities analyst at JPMorgan, noted in her latest report that the adjustment mechanism of this round of the energy crisis is undergoing a fundamental shift—pressure has moved from the crude oil sector to downstream refined product markets. Since the outbreak of hostilities, refined oil prices in Asia have surged 1.5 to 3 times higher than crude oil prices, with aviation fuel crack spreads skyrocketing to extreme levels of $80 to $100 per barrel.

Previously, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned in April that European aviation fuel inventories could be depleted within as little as six weeks, while the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) has formally invoked force majeure clauses to suspend some shipments.

Consumers do not purchase crude oil; they buy fuel. This seemingly simple fact is becoming the core logic for understanding the next phase of the current energy crisis. JPMorgan believes that against the backdrop of constrained refining capacity and a sharp decline in Middle Eastern refined product exports, refined product prices—not crude oil prices—will become the primary channel for demand destruction, delivering substantial impacts on global aviation, logistics, and consumer sectors.

Inventory: The largest supply gap in history, yet crude oil prices remain unusually calm.

More than two months after the outbreak of this conflict, the market faces a paradox that has puzzled analysts: this is recorded as 'the largest crude oil supply disruption in history,' yet Brent crude oil prices have remained around just $100 per barrel.

Data from JPMorgan shows that global crude oil inventories are experiencing the steepest decline on record. If the current trend persists, inventories will reach 'operational stress' levels within weeks and fall to 'operational minimums' by September.

Kaneva explained in the report that the relative stability of oil prices is not due to market indifference to the crisis but rather reflects the acknowledgment of a graver reality: a supply shock of this magnitude cannot be absorbed by the crude oil market alone; the system lacks sufficient elasticity. Refiners in Asia and Europe have been forced to cut operating rates—by 2.1 million barrels per day in March, expanding further to 3.8 million barrels per day in April. Meanwhile, the Middle East itself has lost approximately 4.7 million barrels per day in refined product exports.

According to a Bloomberg report in April, the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) has officially notified customers of invoking force majeure clauses, suspending crude oil and refined product deliveries to vessels unable to enter the Persian Gulf. Informed sources revealed that Kuwait's oil and gas infrastructure has suffered multiple strikes, with current production falling to historic lows last seen in the early 1990s. Even if the conflict ends, full capacity recovery will take time.

Refining Dynamics: A zero-sum game, a molecular battle among products.

To understand why the refined oil crisis is difficult to resolve quickly, it is necessary to comprehend the physical constraints inherent in the refining process itself.

JPMorgan provided a detailed explanation of the operational logic of refining in its report: refining essentially involves separating a barrel of crude oil into different products based on boiling points, forming a strictly mass-conserving system—what goes in must come out, and nothing can be created out of thin air. This means that refining is a zero-sum game; producing more of one type of fuel necessarily implies producing less of another.

Crude oil itself is not a homogeneous substance. Light crude oil molecules are smaller and naturally inclined toward producing gasoline and naphtha, while heavy crude oil molecules are more complex, yielding more diesel, fuel oil, and residue. In highly complex refineries (such as those in the United States), the gasoline yield can be increased from about 20% in its natural state to over 45% through fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) units, as modern refineries are generally deeply optimized for gasoline production due to the large global passenger vehicle fleet.

Jet fuel occupies the "middle distillate" position between gasoline and diesel in the distillation tower, typically accounting for 8% to 15% of refinery output. Diesel also belongs to the middle distillates, representing approximately 25% to 35%. The key issue is that jet fuel and diesel compete for the same batch of molecules in the barrel, creating direct competition in production. Refineries have extremely limited flexibility in adjusting between the two, typically able to shift only about 2% to 5% of total output.

This implies that when market signals require refineries to maximize jet fuel production, diesel supply will almost inevitably suffer.

Impact: A chain reaction, spreading from refineries to gas stations, is already underway.

The signal from current crack spreads is clear enough: jet fuel crack spreads have surged to $80–$100 per barrel, reaching record highs since the Russia-Ukraine conflict, sending an unequivocal directive to refineries—to produce as much jet fuel as possible.

U.S. refineries have responded by increasing jet fuel yields by approximately 2 percentage points and pushing jet fuel exports to record levels to capture excess profits in the global market. However, the costs have quickly become apparent: gasoline yields have dropped by 2 percentage points, with production falling by about 340,000 barrels per day compared to the same period last year. The timing is particularly unfavorable—the peak driving season in the U.S. will officially begin around Memorial Day at the end of May, and retail gasoline prices have already risen to $4.56 per gallon, making the risk of reaching $5 impossible to ignore.

On the aviation side, the impact is equally direct. The IEA has warned that several European countries may begin to face jet fuel shortages within the next six weeks, with the Middle East previously accounting for 75% of Europe’s net jet fuel imports. Low-cost airline EasyJet has indicated that rising fuel costs are weighing on customer bookings, with ticket sales for later this year declining by 2% compared to 2025. ACI Europe, the industry organization representing EU airports, has warned that the summer travel peak will be disrupted, posing a "severe economic shock" to member states reliant on tourism.

JPMorgan concludes that the next phase of the energy shock will no longer manifest as a classic spike in crude oil prices but will instead resemble a refined product and end-user fuel shortage crisis. Crude oil prices may remain relatively stable near $100, while refined product crack spreads continue to widen, directly impacting consumers, airlines, and logistics systems through higher fuel prices.
